transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-11
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE); Marcus Ortega (Redwood SE); Priya Menon (Cardinal Head of ML); Daniel Chu (Platform Eng); Aisha Khan (Security); Tom Reeves (Product)

Summary: Intro/discovery for Dedicated reserved GPU needs. Customer evaluating Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted for production gen/chat workloads. Key topics: isolation (network, tenant), reserved capacity sizing, burst to hosted, autoscaling policies, SLAs and cost tradeoffs, compliance requirements (SOC2, SSO/KMS), and proposed pilot/benchmarking approach.

Topics: dedicated sizing, burst strategy, isolation, telemetry/audit logs, cost modeling, rollout plan

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Lena (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, quick intros — I'm Lena, I'm the account lead. Marcus is our solutions engineer, he'll take the deep dive. Priya, would you like to start with a quick context on what you're trying to solve?
[00:18] Priya (Cardinal): Yeah hi, thanks. So we're building a clinical note summarization pipeline plus an in-app chat for clinicians. We're in late-stage eval for inference infra — currently prototype on a small k8s cluster with some hugging models. Main asks: predictable latency, data isolation for PHI, and being able to do bursts when load spikes — like end of quarter when docs import.
[00:36] Marcus (Redwood SE): Great, that helps. When you say predictable, what's your p95 or p99 SLO look like today?
[00:43] Priya (Cardinal): We want p95 sub-500ms on 512 tokens for the summary flows. Chat can tolerate up to 1.2s p95. But consistency is key — if we see a 2–3x regression at peak it's bad.
[00:56] Daniel (Platform): And we need tenancy isolation — the model can't share GPU with external tenants handling PHI. So reserved capacity or private deployment is preferred.
[01:06] Lena (Redwood AE): Understood. That's exactly what Dedicated is targeted for — reserved GPU pools with isolation. Marcus, can you explain the reserved vs burst behavior?
[01:15] Marcus (Redwood SE): Yeah. So with Redwood Dedicated you reserve a pool — for example N nodes with X A100 80s — that's single-tenant from a compute perspective. You can configure autoscaling policies for intra-pool scaling and then we have burst-to-hosted: when your dedicated pool is saturated, visits can spill over to our hosted fleet to maintain availability. Bursts are controlled by policy and by model variant compatibility.
[01:36] Tom (Product): Quick question — when bursting to hosted, does customer data ever leave the VPC boundary?
[01:41] Marcus (Redwood SE): Short answer: yes, it will leave the dedicated customer's compute if you allow burst. We have a private-link style option for dedicated that reduces egress exposure, but burst-to-hosted inherently routes to Redwood-managed infrastructure. For PHI that may be a hard no — in which case we can set strict policies to queue or reject.
[01:56] Aisha (Security): Right, so we need to confirm that. Our initial compliance posture requires no egress to shared multi-tenant compute unless it's tokenized/non-PHI. We also need KMS integration and audit logs.
[02:08] Lena (Redwood AE): Got it. We'll flag that for the security workshop. Marcus, can you talk on capacity planning — single model qps and how to size?
[02:17] Marcus (Redwood SE): Sure. We usually start with throughput numbers for the model family — e.g., a 13B model quantized to int8 on an A100 80 gives X tokens/s (note: rough numbers here). We ask for expected concurrent users, average tokens per call, and traffic profile (burstiness). For example, if you expect 200 concurrent summarization requests at peak with 512 tokens avg and target p95 500ms, that maps to roughly Y GPU-equivalents — we'll run a benchmark to get an exact recommended vCPUs/GPU count.
[02:49] Priya (Cardinal): Our rough numbers: 100–200 concurrent summarizers, plus 30–50 chat sessions. Peak QPS for token generation maybe 800–1,200 tokens/s for a sustained 10–15 minute window during imports.
[03:04] Marcus (Redwood SE): OK that helps. Sounds like you'd start with a modest dedicated pool and enable controlled burst to hosted for non-PHI traffic. But if PHI must never leave, we recommend a larger reserved footprint or Private on-prem/air-gapped.
[03:18] Daniel (Platform): What's the billing model for reserved? Monthly commit? Hourly overage if we burst?
[03:24] Lena (Redwood AE): Reserved is a monthly commitment with options for annual. You pay for the reserved capacity even if you don't use it (that's the guarantee). For burst into hosted, there are overage rates that apply per-token or per-invocation depending on how you route. We'll send a worksheet with cost scenarios.
[03:38] Aisha (Security): On the SLA — if you advertise latency SLOs for dedicated, are those covered in the contract? We need p99 SLAs where possible and credits for violations.
[03:47] Marcus (Redwood SE): We have SLA tiers for Dedicated customers; p99 latency targets are part of higher tiers. There are also observability hooks — per-route latency, token-level billing, trace IDs. We can also set fallback policies and automatic rollbacks to smaller models to maintain availability.
[03:59] Priya (Cardinal): Could you explain the fallback/rollout story? We need deterministic behavior in incident scenarios.
[04:05] Marcus (Redwood SE): Sure. In Redwood, a route can have a list of model variants with policies. If the primary model can't be scheduled due to capacity, we can either queue, fail, or route to a cheaper/quantized variant. Also can route to local cache if prefix hits. For clinical text we typically avoid model downgrades without approval — that's a policy decision.
[04:26] Tom (Product): How does the KV cache and prefix caching work in a multi-tenant dedicated pool? Any cross-tenant leakage risk?
[04:33] Marcus (Redwood SE): No cross-tenant leakage — caches are scoped per-customer/route. The KV cache is per-instance and we scrub and TTL. The tricky bit is warm caches after scale-up vs cold starts — which affect p95. We can pre-warm KV caches as part of the deployment plan.
[04:50] Daniel (Platform): We care about autoscaling cold-starts. If you spin up new nodes, how long to be ready?
[04:56] Marcus (Redwood SE): Cold start depends on model size and whether you use shared-preload. Typical cold start for a 70B model could be several minutes; for 13B it's often under 90s if images are cached. Dedicated pools can be configured with spare nodes (buffer) to handle minute-scale spikes.
[05:12] Priya (Cardinal): Another question — network isolation. We want private VPC peering and control-plane visibility. How integrated is Redwood Private control plane for Dedicated customers?
[05:22] Lena (Redwood AE): For Dedicated we offer VPC peering and private networking options. The Private product is a step further — private control plane and on-prem if needed. For your case, Dedicated with VPC and strict non-burst policies might be enough, unless you require full air-gap.
[05:36] Aisha (Security): We also need SSO/SAML, RBAC, and audit trails. Can you surface those logs to our SIEM?
[05:43] Marcus (Redwood SE): Yes — audit logs and event streams can be exported to your logging endpoints (CloudWatch, Splunk, etc.). RBAC integrates with SAML/SCIM. We'll share the docs.
[05:54] Priya (Cardinal): On model updates and rollouts — we need version pinning and canary rollout to a % of traffic. Do you support that?
[06:01] Marcus (Redwood SE): Yep, canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic rollback on quality regressions tied to eval prompt sets. We also maintain model version pins per route.
[06:12] Tom (Product): Cost question — do you have recommended quantization or batch strategies to reduce costs without sacrificing our clinical quality?
[06:19] Marcus (Redwood SE): We provide Optimize recommendations — quantization profiles per model family, batching suggestions based on latency targets, and caching advice. For clinical accuracy, many customers run small eval suites to verify quantization doesn't regress key metrics. We can help set that up in the pilot.
[06:36] Priya (Cardinal): For the pilot — we want dedicated pool sized for 2–3 baseline nodes, run a set of 1h soak tests plus a synthetic 15-min spike. Can Redwood run that on our behalf or provide a runbook?
[06:48] Marcus (Redwood SE): Yes, we'll run benchmarks with your sample prompts and dataset. We'll also give you a runbook to reproduce locally. Our plan: baseline latency/throughput, then spike test with burst allowed/blocked, and evaluate costs.
[07:00] Daniel (Platform): If we block burst — will requests queue and cause user-facing timeouts?
[07:05] Marcus (Redwood SE): If you block burst and the dedicated pool is full, you can choose to queue with a timeout, fail fast with an explicit error, or route to a best-effort local fallback. We generally recommend queue + short timeout for user flows where retries are acceptable.
[07:18] Aisha (Security): We need to walk through data residency — logs or telemetry that include PII must stay in region. Does Redwood support region pinning for Dedicated?
[07:27] Lena (Redwood AE): Yes, Dedicated has region constraints; we can pin the pool to a specific region and prevent cross-region routing. We'll capture your region requirement in the follow-ups.
[07:37] Priya (Cardinal): Thought on burst economics — if we reserve too much, we'll waste money; if too little, we risk failed requests. What's the recommended buffer percent?
[07:45] Marcus (Redwood SE): Typical recommendation is a 20–50% buffer depending on spike patterns. For very spiky workloads short spikes are handled by burst-to-hosted, for PHI-bound flows aim for higher buffer or Private deployment. We'll model scenarios in the pricing worksheet.
[07:59] Tom (Product): Any customers similar to us in healthcare using Dedicated with strict non-egress policies?
[08:06] Lena (Redwood AE): We have a couple of regulated customers in medtech who use Dedicated + VPC with strict no-burst flags and larger reserved pools. We can anonymize references and set an intro if useful.
[08:17] Priya (Cardinal): Ok good. On dev workflows — what's the lifecycle to push a new model: dev -> canary -> prod? How long for rollout?
[08:25] Marcus (Redwood SE): Dev workflows are typically CI-based: build container/weights, push to registry, create model version in Redwood, then route updates via canary percent. Rollout times depend on model loads and whether new nodes are required; small model swaps can be minutes, large model brings could take longer.
[08:40] Daniel (Platform): We also want to understand observability integration — can we get token-level billing by route? We need to attribute cost to product teams.
[08:47] Marcus (Redwood SE): Yes, Redwood Console gives token-level cost breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and you can tag routes to map to internal cost centers.
[08:56] Priya (Cardinal): A few nitty gritty items — Do you support HSM/KMS with customer-managed keys for model artifacts and logs?
[09:04] Marcus (Redwood SE): Yes we support KMS integrations and can work with customer-managed keys for keys in transit at rest. HSM integrations depend on the deployment mode; Private has strongest guarantees. We'll detail this in the security doc we share.
[09:16] Tom (Product): Let's talk timeline. We're aiming to be production-ready by end of Q2. What is a realistic pilot-to-prod path?
[09:23] Lena (Redwood AE): Pilot in 2–3 weeks, if pilot ok then dedicated reservation procurement + foam lead time — we typically see 3–6 weeks for dedicated capacity to stabilize depending on contract and infra readiness. So end of Q2 is tight but feasible with fast procurement.
[09:38] Priya (Cardinal): Procurement and legal will need a security review — can you share SOC2 + contract redlines beforehand?
[09:44] Lena (Redwood AE): Yes we'll send SOC2 link and a sample contract. Marcus, anything else for the benchmarks?
[09:50] Marcus (Redwood SE): I'll include test plan: baseline latency/throughput (per model size), KV cache warm vs cold, spike test with controlled ramp, and a PHI-safe flow to validate non-burst. We also test fallback policies.
[10:04] Daniel (Platform): For the pilot, we'll probably allow non-PHI traffic to burst but block PHI. How do we flag requests as PHI vs non-PHI at routing?
[10:12] Marcus (Redwood SE): You can mark routes or tag requests via headers/metadata. The Redwood router honors route-level policies. So you might have a /clinical route with allow_burst=false and a /public route with allow_burst=true.
[10:25] Priya (Cardinal): One more — if we need to scale our dedicated pool quickly, what's the procurement lead time? Are there fast lanes?
[10:32] Lena (Redwood AE): We do have burst capacity add-ons and reserved increases that can be procured faster; depends on available capacity in the region. We'll include that in the pricing worksheet and call out expected lead times.
[10:45] Tom (Product): Ok let's recap next steps before we run out of time.
[10:49] Lena (Redwood AE): Recap: Redwood to send pricing worksheet and SOC2 + security docs; Marcus to share benchmark plan; Cardinal to confirm pilot dataset and compliance reviewers; schedule pilot kickoff week of April 21. Any other items?
[10:59] Priya (Cardinal): Sounds right. Also please include a clear statement on burst-egress policy for PHI and confirm region pinning.
[11:06] Aisha (Security): And add RBAC/SCIM doc and audit log retention options.
[11:10] Lena (Redwood AE): Will do. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.
[11:16] END OF MEETING
